name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_UNIT6_Q01 - Abundance of aluminium in earth crust

questiontext.text: Which metal is the most abundant metal and the third most abundant element in the earth's crust (approximately \(8.3\%\) by weight)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Elements vary in abundance in the earth's crust. Among metals, abundance is led by light metals that form major rock-forming minerals such as mica and clays.

Step 2: Evaluation
Aluminium is the most abundant metal in the earth's crust and ranks as the third most abundant element overall at about \(8.3\%\) by weight. Iron is the second most abundant metal.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Aluminium is the most abundant metal and the third most abundant element in the earth's crust.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_UNIT6_Q02 - Impurities present in ruby and sapphire

questiontext.text: The gemstones 'ruby' and 'sapphire' are impure forms of \(\mathrm{Al_2O_3}\) containing which transition metal impurities, respectively?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Many gemstones are crystalline \(\mathrm{Al_2O_3}\) (corundum) whose characteristic colours arise from trace transition metal impurities.

Step 2: Evaluation
Ruby is an impure form of \(\mathrm{Al_2O_3}\) containing chromium (\(\mathrm{Cr}\)) as impurity, whereas sapphire contains cobalt (\(\mathrm{Co}\)) as impurity.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Ruby and sapphire contain \(\mathrm{Cr}\) and \(\mathrm{Co}\) respectively as impurities.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_UNIT6_Q03 - Distinction between minerals and ores

questiontext.text: Which statement accurately distinguishes an ore from a mineral?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Metals occur in the earth's crust in naturally occurring chemical substances obtained through mining, called minerals.

Step 2: Evaluation
Out of the many minerals in which a metal may be found, only those from which the metal can be extracted chemically feasibly and commercially viably are termed ores. Hence, all ores are minerals, but not all minerals are ores.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
An ore is a mineral that is commercially viable and chemically feasible to be used as a source for extracting a metal.

answer.text: Every mineral found in the earth's crust is classified as an ore.
Ores are always free of earthly impurities, whereas minerals contain gangue.
Ores are those specific minerals from which a metal can be extracted profitably and feasibly.
Minerals are synthetic compounds, whereas ores occur naturally.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_UNIT6_Q04 - Iron ore avoided due to sulphur dioxide pollution

questiontext.text: Which mineral of iron is generally avoided for the commercial extraction of iron because it produces polluting \(\mathrm{SO_2}\) gas during processing?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
For the extraction of iron, abundant oxide ores are preferred over sulphide ores to avoid environmental pollution from sulphur dioxide gas.

Step 2: Evaluation
Haematite (\(\mathrm{Fe_2O_3}\)), magnetite (\(\mathrm{Fe_3O_4}\)), and siderite (\(\mathrm{FeCO_3}\)) do not contain sulphur, whereas iron pyrites (\(\mathrm{FeS_2}\)) is a sulphide mineral that releases polluting \(\mathrm{SO_2}\) gas when heated in air.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Iron pyrites (\(\mathrm{FeS_2}\)) is avoided for iron extraction because it produces polluting \(\mathrm{SO_2}\) gas.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_UNIT6_Q05 - Chemical composition of copper pyrites and malachite

questiontext.text: What are the chemical compositions of copper pyrites and malachite, respectively?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Copper occurs in nature as sulphide, oxide, and basic carbonate ores.

Step 2: Evaluation
Copper pyrites is a mixed sulphide of copper and iron with formula \(\mathrm{CuFeS_2}\), while malachite is a basic copper carbonate with formula \(\mathrm{CuCO_3 \cdot Cu(OH)_2}\). By comparison, \(\mathrm{Cu_2S}\) is copper glance and \(\mathrm{Cu_2O}\) is cuprite.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Copper pyrites and malachite have the compositions \(\mathrm{CuFeS_2}\) and \(\mathrm{CuCO_3 \cdot Cu(OH)_2}\), respectively.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_UNIT6_Q06 - Definition of gangue in metallurgy

questiontext.text: The earthly or undesired materials such as sand and clay that contaminate an ore are known as:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Mined ores rarely contain only the desired metal-bearing mineral and are mixed with rocky or earthly impurities.

Step 2: Evaluation
These earthly or undesired contaminants (such as sand and clay) are called gangue. Flux is a substance added during smelting to combine with gangue and form fusible slag, while anode mud is the insoluble residue deposited beneath the anode during electrolytic refining.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The earthly or undesired materials contaminating an ore are known as gangue.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_UNIT6_Q07 - Ancient Indian downward distillation technique

questiontext.text: In ancient India, the sophisticated 'downward' distillation technique mastered at Zawar in Rajasthan was specifically used to produce which pair of low-boiling metals?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Metals with low boiling points tend to vaporise during smelting of their ores, requiring condensation of the metal vapour in a separate container.

Step 2: Evaluation
Archaeological evidence from Zawar in Rajasthan (6th–5th century BCE) shows that Indian metallurgists were the first to master zinc distillation using a downward distillation technique in which zinc vapour was condensed in a lower container. This technique was also applied to mercury.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The downward distillation technique was used for zinc and mercury.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_UNIT6_Q08 - Composition of Delhi Iron Pillar wrought iron

questiontext.text: The ancient Iron Pillar in Delhi, an example of corrosion-resistant wrought iron exposed to the atmosphere for about 1,600 years, has which notable non-iron elemental composition by weight?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Wrought iron produced by solid-state reduction and hot forging in ancient India had low carbon and a characteristic phosphorus content that contributed to its remarkable resistance to corrosion.

Step 2: Evaluation
The average weight percentage composition of components besides iron in the Delhi Iron Pillar is \(0.15\%\,\mathrm{C}\), \(0.05\%\,\mathrm{Si}\), \(0.05\%\,\mathrm{Mn}\), \(0.25\%\,\mathrm{P}\), \(0.005\%\,\mathrm{Ni}\), \(0.03\%\,\mathrm{Cu}\), and \(0.02\%\,\mathrm{N}\). By contrast, Wootz steel contains \(1.0\text{--}1.9\%\,\mathrm{C}\), cast iron contains about \(3\%\,\mathrm{C}\), and pig iron contains about \(4\%\,\mathrm{C}\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The wrought iron of the Delhi Iron Pillar contains \(0.15\%\,\mathrm{C}\) and \(0.25\%\,\mathrm{P}\) along with minor amounts of \(\mathrm{Si}\), \(\mathrm{Mn}\), \(\mathrm{Ni}\), \(\mathrm{Cu}\), and \(\mathrm{N}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_UNIT6_Q09 - Characteristics of ancient Indian Wootz steel

questiontext.text: Which statement regarding ancient Indian Wootz steel is correct?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Ancient India was a major innovator in high-grade steel manufacture using the crucible process, in which iron, charcoal, and glass were heated together until the iron melted and absorbed carbon.

Step 2: Evaluation
Wootz steel (derived from the word 'ukku' used for steel in Karnataka and Andhra Pradesh) is primarily iron containing a high proportion of carbon (\(1.0\text{--}1.9\%\)). It was exported to Europe, China, and the Arab world, where it became known as Damascus steel.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Wootz steel is primarily iron containing \(1.0\text{--}1.9\%\) carbon, manufactured by the crucible process and derived from the word 'ukku'.

answer.text: It is primarily iron containing \(1.0\text{--}1.9\%\) carbon and was known in the Middle East as Damascus steel.
It is an alloy of gold and silver discovered at Mohenjodaro.
It is porous sponge iron obtained by solid-state reduction without melting.
It is an alloy of copper and zinc produced by downward distillation.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_UNIT6_Q10 - Identifying non-zinc ore among given minerals

questiontext.text: Which of the following is NOT an ore of zinc?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Principal ores of zinc include its sulphide, carbonate, and oxide minerals.

Step 2: Evaluation
Zinc blende or sphalerite (\(\mathrm{ZnS}\)), calamine (\(\mathrm{ZnCO_3}\)), and zincite (\(\mathrm{ZnO}\)) are all ores of zinc. Siderite (\(\mathrm{FeCO_3}\)), however, is a carbonate ore of iron.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Siderite is not an ore of zinc; it is an ore of iron.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_UNIT6_Q11 - Principle of hydraulic washing

questiontext.text: Hydraulic washing is a method of concentrating ores that is based on the difference in:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Ore concentration methods exploit differences in physical or chemical properties between the metal-bearing mineral and the gangue.

Step 2: Evaluation
Hydraulic washing is a type of gravity separation based on the difference between the specific gravities of the ore and the gangue particles. When an upward stream of running water washes the powdered ore, the lighter gangue particles are washed away while the heavier ore particles are left behind.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Hydraulic washing is based on the difference in specific gravities of the ore and the gangue particles.

answer.text: Magnetic susceptibilities of the ore and the gangue
Solubilities of the ore and the gangue in aqueous alkali
Specific gravities of the ore and the gangue particles
Boiling points of the ore and the gangue

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_UNIT6_Q12 - Ores concentrated by magnetic separation

questiontext.text: Which set of ores can be concentrated using the magnetic separation method?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Magnetic separation is applicable when either the ore or the gangue is attracted towards a magnetic field.

Step 2: Evaluation
Ores containing iron—such as haematite (\(\mathrm{Fe_2O_3}\)), magnetite (\(\mathrm{Fe_3O_4}\)), siderite (\(\mathrm{FeCO_3}\)), and iron pyrites (\(\mathrm{FeS_2}\))—are magnetic, so non-magnetic impurities can be separated from them using a magnetic roller. Bauxite, zinc blende, and calamine are non-magnetic and are concentrated by leaching, froth floatation, or other methods.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Haematite, magnetite, and siderite can be concentrated by magnetic separation.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_UNIT6_Q13 - Type of ores concentrated by froth floatation

questiontext.text: The froth floatation method is primarily used for removing gangue from which type of ores?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Froth floatation relies on the preferential wetting of mineral particles by oil and of gangue particles by water.

Step 2: Evaluation
Sulphide ores (such as \(\mathrm{ZnS}\), \(\mathrm{PbS}\), and \(\mathrm{CuFeS_2}\)) are preferentially wetted by oils (enhanced by collectors) and carried into the froth by air bubbles, leaving earthly gangue in water.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Froth floatation is primarily used for concentrating sulphide ores.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_UNIT6_Q14 - Examples of froth stabilisers and collectors

questiontext.text: In the froth floatation process, which pair correctly represents a collector and a froth stabiliser, respectively?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Froth floatation uses collectors to enhance the non-wettability of mineral particles and froth stabilisers to stabilise the froth formed by agitation with air.

Step 2: Evaluation
Examples of collectors include pine oils, fatty acids, and xanthates. Examples of froth stabilisers include cresols and aniline. Sodium cyanide (\(\mathrm{NaCN}\)) acts as a depressant, while cryolite (\(\mathrm{Na_3AlF_6}\)) is used in the electrolytic extraction of aluminium.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Pine oil (or xanthates) is a collector and aniline (or cresols) is a froth stabiliser.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_UNIT6_Q15 - Role of depressant in separating ZnS and PbS

questiontext.text: When an ore contains both \(\mathrm{ZnS}\) and \(\mathrm{PbS}\), how does \(\mathrm{NaCN}\) help separate the two sulphides during froth floatation?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Two sulphide ores can be separated by adjusting the oil-to-water proportion or by adding a depressant that selectively alters the surface behaviour of one sulphide.

Step 2: Evaluation
In a mixture of \(\mathrm{ZnS}\) and \(\mathrm{PbS}\), \(\mathrm{NaCN}\) acts as a depressant. It selectively prevents \(\mathrm{ZnS}\) from coming into the froth while allowing \(\mathrm{PbS}\) to rise with the froth.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
\(\mathrm{NaCN}\) selectively prevents \(\mathrm{ZnS}\) from entering the froth while allowing \(\mathrm{PbS}\) to come with the froth.

answer.text: It selectively prevents \(\mathrm{PbS}\) from entering the froth while allowing \(\mathrm{ZnS}\) to float.
It selectively prevents \(\mathrm{ZnS}\) from entering the froth while allowing \(\mathrm{PbS}\) to come with the froth.
It precipitates both \(\mathrm{ZnS}\) and \(\mathrm{PbS}\) at the bottom while gangue floats.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_UNIT6_Q16 - Digestion of bauxite with sodium hydroxide

questiontext.text: During the leaching of alumina from bauxite containing \(\mathrm{SiO_2}\), iron oxides, and \(\mathrm{TiO_2}\), the powdered ore is digested with concentrated \(\mathrm{NaOH}\) at \(473\text{--}523\,\mathrm{K}\) and \(35\text{--}36\,\mathrm{bar}\). Which species dissolve into the aqueous phase during this digestion?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Leaching separates the desired ore component by selectively dissolving it in a suitable solvent while leaving insoluble impurities behind.

Step 2: Evaluation
During digestion of bauxite with concentrated \(\mathrm{NaOH}\) at \(473\text{--}523\,\mathrm{K}\) and \(35\text{--}36\,\mathrm{bar}\), \(\mathrm{Al_2O_3}\) dissolves as sodium aluminate (\(\mathrm{NaAl(OH)_4}\)) and the impurity \(\mathrm{SiO_2}\) also dissolves as sodium silicate. Iron oxides and \(\mathrm{TiO_2}\) remain undissolved and are left behind.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Both \(\mathrm{Al_2O_3}\) (as sodium aluminate) and \(\mathrm{SiO_2}\) (as sodium silicate) dissolve into the aqueous phase during digestion.

answer.text: Only \(\mathrm{Al_2O_3}\) as sodium aluminate; \(\mathrm{SiO_2}\), iron oxides, and \(\mathrm{TiO_2}\) remain undissolved.
Only iron oxides and \(\mathrm{TiO_2}\); \(\mathrm{Al_2O_3}\) remains as a solid residue.
\(\mathrm{Al_2O_3}\), iron oxides, and \(\mathrm{TiO_2}\); only \(\mathrm{SiO_2}\) remains undissolved.
\(\mathrm{Al_2O_3}\) (as sodium aluminate) and \(\mathrm{SiO_2}\) (as sodium silicate); other impurities are left behind.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_UNIT6_Q17 - Neutralisation and seeding of sodium aluminate

questiontext.text: In the purification of bauxite, after digesting the ore with \(\mathrm{NaOH}\), how is hydrated alumina precipitated while keeping sodium silicate in solution?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Sodium aluminate is separated from soluble sodium silicate by controlled neutralisation of the alkaline solution.

Step 2: Evaluation
Passing \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) gas through the sodium aluminate solution neutralises it and precipitates hydrated \(\mathrm{Al_2O_3 \cdot xH_2O}\) according to \(2\mathrm{NaAl(OH)_4} + 2\mathrm{CO_2}(\mathrm{g}) \rightarrow \mathrm{Al_2O_3 \cdot xH_2O}(\mathrm{s}) + 2\mathrm{NaHCO_3}(\mathrm{aq})\). A small amount of freshly prepared hydrated \(\mathrm{Al_2O_3}\) is added (seeding) to induce precipitation, while sodium silicate remains in solution.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Hydrated alumina is precipitated by passing \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) gas and seeding with freshly prepared hydrated \(\mathrm{Al_2O_3}\).

answer.text: By passing \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) gas and seeding with freshly prepared hydrated \(\mathrm{Al_2O_3}\)
By adding zinc dust to displace aluminium metal

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_UNIT6_Q18 - Temperature for dehydrating hydrated alumina

questiontext.text: At what temperature is filtered and dried hydrated alumina (\(\mathrm{Al_2O_3 \cdot xH_2O}\)) heated to obtain pure anhydrous \(\mathrm{Al_2O_3}\)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
After precipitation and filtration, hydrated alumina must be thermally dehydrated to obtain pure \(\mathrm{Al_2O_3}\) suitable for electrolysis.

Step 2: Evaluation
As represented by \(\mathrm{Al_2O_3 \cdot xH_2O}(\mathrm{s}) \xrightarrow{1470\,\mathrm{K}} \mathrm{Al_2O_3}(\mathrm{s}) + x\mathrm{H_2O}(\mathrm{g})\), hydrated alumina is heated to \(1470\,\mathrm{K}\) to drive off water and give back pure \(\mathrm{Al_2O_3}\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Pure \(\mathrm{Al_2O_3}\) is obtained by heating hydrated alumina at \(1470\,\mathrm{K}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_UNIT6_Q19 - Redox roles in cyanide leaching of silver and gold

questiontext.text: In the extraction of silver and gold by leaching with dilute \(\mathrm{NaCN}\) in the presence of air followed by treatment with zinc, what are the respective roles of \(\mathrm{O_2}\) and \(\mathrm{Zn}\)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Cyanide leaching of noble metals (\(\mathrm{M} = \mathrm{Ag}\) or \(\mathrm{Au}\)) involves an initial oxidation step to form a soluble dicyano complex, followed by a reductive displacement step.

Step 2: Evaluation of the Reactions
In the first reaction, \(4\mathrm{M}(\mathrm{s}) + 8\mathrm{CN^-}(\mathrm{aq}) + 2\mathrm{H_2O}(\mathrm{aq}) + \mathrm{O_2}(\mathrm{g}) \rightarrow 4[\mathrm{M(CN)_2}]^-(\mathrm{aq}) + 4\mathrm{OH^-}(\mathrm{aq})\), the metal is oxidised from \(0\) to \(+1\) oxidation state by \(\mathrm{O_2}\), so \(\mathrm{O_2}\) acts as an oxidising agent. In the second reaction, \(2[\mathrm{M(CN)_2}]^-(\mathrm{aq}) + \mathrm{Zn}(\mathrm{s}) \rightarrow [\mathrm{Zn(CN)_4}]^{2-}(\mathrm{aq}) + 2\mathrm{M}(\mathrm{s})\), zinc reduces \(\mathrm{M}^+\) back to metallic \(\mathrm{M}\) while itself being oxidised to \(\mathrm{Zn}^{2+}\), so \(\mathrm{Zn}\) acts as a reducing agent.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
\(\mathrm{O_2}\) acts as an oxidising agent and \(\mathrm{Zn}\) acts as a reducing agent.

answer.text: \(\mathrm{O_2}\) acts as a reducing agent and \(\mathrm{Zn}\) acts as an oxidising agent.
\(\mathrm{O_2}\) acts as an oxidising agent and \(\mathrm{Zn}\) acts as a reducing agent.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_UNIT6_Q20 - Stoichiometry of gold leaching with cyanide

questiontext.text: According to the balanced equation for the leaching of gold with cyanide in the presence of air, how many moles of \(\mathrm{CN^-}\) and \(\mathrm{O_2}\), respectively, are required to leach \(1\,\mathrm{mol}\) of \(\mathrm{Au}\)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
We are asked to find the moles of \(\mathrm{CN^-}\) and \(\mathrm{O_2}\) required to leach \(1\,\mathrm{mol}\) of \(\mathrm{Au}\) using dilute cyanide solution and air.

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
All reactants react completely according to the standard stoichiometric equation for gold leaching.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
The balanced chemical equation for gold leaching is:
\(4\mathrm{Au}(\mathrm{s}) + 8\mathrm{CN^-}(\mathrm{aq}) + 2\mathrm{H_2O}(\mathrm{aq}) + \mathrm{O_2}(\mathrm{g}) \rightarrow 4[\mathrm{Au(CN)_2}]^-(\mathrm{aq}) + 4\mathrm{OH^-}(\mathrm{aq})\).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
From the balanced equation, \(4\,\mathrm{mol}\) of \(\mathrm{Au}\) require \(8\,\mathrm{mol}\) of \(\mathrm{CN^-}\) and \(1\,\mathrm{mol}\) of \(\mathrm{O_2}\).
Dividing the stoichiometric coefficients by \(4\) to obtain the amounts per \(1\,\mathrm{mol}\) of \(\mathrm{Au}\):
Moles of \(\mathrm{CN^-} = \frac{8}{4} = 2\,\mathrm{mol}\).
Moles of \(\mathrm{O_2} = \frac{1}{4} = 0.25\,\mathrm{mol}\).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Checking atom and charge balance for \(1\,\mathrm{mol}\) of \(\mathrm{Au}\): \(\mathrm{Au} + 2\mathrm{CN^-} + \frac{1}{2}\mathrm{H_2O} + \frac{1}{4}\mathrm{O_2} \rightarrow [\mathrm{Au(CN)_2}]^- + \mathrm{OH^-}\), which balances both atoms and \(-2\) charge on each side. Thus, \(2\,\mathrm{mol}\) of \(\mathrm{CN^-}\) and \(0.25\,\mathrm{mol}\) of \(\mathrm{O_2}\) are required.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_UNIT6_Q21 - Reason for converting sulphide ores to oxides

questiontext.text: Why are sulphide ores usually converted into oxides before reduction to the metal?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Isolation of a metal from its concentrated ore involves converting it into a form suitable for reduction, followed by reduction to the metal.

Step 2: Evaluation
Metal oxides are thermodynamically much easier to reduce (for example, using \(\mathrm{C}\) or \(\mathrm{CO}\)) than metal sulphides, as also seen from Ellingham diagrams for oxides versus sulphides.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Sulphide ores are converted to oxides before reduction because metal oxides are easier to reduce than metal sulphides.

answer.text: Oxides are easier to reduce than sulphides.
Oxides have higher melting points than sulphides.
Sulphides cannot react with any reducing agent at any temperature.
Converting sulphides to oxides increases the gangue content for slag formation.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_UNIT6_Q22 - Identifying a calcination reaction

questiontext.text: Which of the following chemical reactions represents calcination?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Calcination involves heating an ore to remove volatile matter such as water or carbon dioxide, leaving behind the metal oxide.

Step 2: Evaluation
Thermal decomposition of dolomite, \(\mathrm{CaCO_3 \cdot MgCO_3}(\mathrm{s}) \xrightarrow{\Delta} \mathrm{CaO}(\mathrm{s}) + \mathrm{MgO}(\mathrm{s}) + 2\mathrm{CO_2}(\mathrm{g})\), removes \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) as volatile matter and leaves behind metal oxides, which is calcination. Heating \(\mathrm{ZnS}\), \(\mathrm{PbS}\), or \(\mathrm{Cu_2S}\) in a regular supply of air to form oxides and \(\mathrm{SO_2}\) represents roasting.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The thermal decomposition \(\mathrm{CaCO_3 \cdot MgCO_3}(\mathrm{s}) \xrightarrow{\Delta} \mathrm{CaO}(\mathrm{s}) + \mathrm{MgO}(\mathrm{s}) + 2\mathrm{CO_2}(\mathrm{g})\) represents calcination.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_UNIT6_Q23 - Conditions for roasting of sulphide ores

questiontext.text: During the process of roasting, a sulphide ore is heated in a furnace:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Roasting is an oxidative thermal treatment used to convert sulphide ores into metal oxides.

Step 2: Evaluation
In roasting, the ore is heated in a regular supply of air in a furnace at a temperature below the melting point of the metal, producing metal oxides and \(\mathrm{SO_2}\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Roasting involves heating the ore in a regular supply of air at a temperature below the melting point of the metal.

answer.text: In the absence of air above the boiling point of the metal
In an aqueous solution of sodium hydroxide under high pressure
In a regular supply of air at a temperature below the melting point of the metal
With carbon monoxide in a closed vessel above the melting point of the metal

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_UNIT6_Q24 - Utilisation of sulphur dioxide from roasting

questiontext.text: The \(\mathrm{SO_2}\) gas produced during the roasting of sulphide ores is industrially utilised for manufacturing:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Roasting of sulphide ores such as \(\mathrm{ZnS}\), \(\mathrm{PbS}\), and \(\mathrm{Cu_2S}\) generates \(\mathrm{SO_2}\) as a by-product.

Step 2: Evaluation
Rather than releasing \(\mathrm{SO_2}\) into the atmosphere, it is captured and utilised for the manufacture of sulphuric acid (\(\mathrm{H_2SO_4}\)).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The \(\mathrm{SO_2}\) produced during roasting is utilised for manufacturing \(\mathrm{H_2SO_4}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_UNIT6_Q25 - Role of silica in metallurgy of copper

questiontext.text: What is the role of silica (\(\mathrm{SiO_2}\)) in the metallurgy of copper?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Copper sulphide ores often contain iron as an impurity, which oxidises to \(\mathrm{FeO}\) during heating.

Step 2: Evaluation
Silica (\(\mathrm{SiO_2}\)) is added as a flux in the reverberatory furnace and converter to combine with basic iron oxide (\(\mathrm{FeO}\)) and remove it as fusible iron silicate slag: \(\mathrm{FeO} + \mathrm{SiO_2} \rightarrow \mathrm{FeSiO_3}\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Silica acts as a flux to remove iron oxide impurity as iron silicate (\(\mathrm{FeSiO_3}\)) slag.

answer.text: It acts as a flux to remove iron oxide as \(\mathrm{FeSiO_3}\) slag.
It acts as a reducing agent to reduce \(\mathrm{Cu_2O}\) to metallic copper.
It acts as a collector in froth floatation of copper pyrites.
It acts as an electrolyte in the refining of blister copper.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_UNIT6_Q26 - Thermodynamic criterion for thermal reduction

questiontext.text: What is the thermodynamic criterion for the feasibility of a thermal reduction of a metal oxide at a given temperature?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
According to thermodynamics, the spontaneity of a chemical process at constant temperature and pressure is governed by its Gibbs energy change, \(\Delta G = \Delta H - T\Delta S\).

Step 2: Evaluation
A thermal reduction reaction proceeds spontaneously at a specified temperature only when the overall Gibbs energy change (\(\Delta G\)) for the coupled reaction is negative (\(\Delta G < 0\)).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The Gibbs energy change (\(\Delta G\)) of the reaction must be negative at that temperature.

answer.text: The enthalpy change (\(\Delta H\)) must be positive.
The Gibbs energy change (\(\Delta G\)) must be negative.
The entropy change (\(\Delta S\)) must be negative.
The Gibbs energy change (\(\Delta G\)) must be equal to zero.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_UNIT6_Q27 - Reason for positive slope in Ellingham diagram

questiontext.text: In an Ellingham diagram (\(\Delta_{\mathrm{r}}G^{\ominus}\) versus \(T\)), why do the curves for the formation of most metal oxides (\(\mathrm{M_xO}(\mathrm{s})\)) have a positive slope?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
For the formation of a solid metal oxide, \(2x\mathrm{M}(\mathrm{s}) + \mathrm{O_2}(\mathrm{g}) \rightarrow 2\mathrm{M}_x\mathrm{O}(\mathrm{s})\), the temperature dependence of \(\Delta_{\mathrm{r}}G^{\ominus}\) is given by \(\Delta_{\mathrm{r}}G^{\ominus} = \Delta_{\mathrm{r}}H^{\ominus} - T\Delta_{\mathrm{r}}S^{\ominus}\).

Step 2: Evaluation
Because gaseous \(\mathrm{O_2}\) is consumed to form a solid oxide, molecular randomness decreases, so \(\Delta S\) is negative. Consequently, the \(-T\Delta S\) term is positive and increases with rising temperature \(T\), shifting \(\Delta_{\mathrm{r}}G^{\ominus}\) to less negative (higher) values and giving a positive slope.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Gaseous oxygen is consumed during oxide formation, making \(\Delta S\) negative and \(-T\Delta S\) positive.

answer.text: Gaseous oxygen is evolved during oxide formation, making \(\Delta S\) positive.
Enthalpy of formation \(\Delta H\) becomes strongly positive as temperature increases.
Gaseous oxygen is consumed during oxide formation, making \(\Delta S\) negative and \(-T\Delta S\) positive.
The equilibrium constant \(K\) increases exponentially with temperature.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_UNIT6_Q28 - Meaning of crossing zero Gibbs energy line

questiontext.text: In an Ellingham diagram, when the \(\Delta_{\mathrm{r}}G^{\ominus}\) versus \(T\) curve for a metal oxide formation crosses the \(\Delta_{\mathrm{r}}G^{\ominus} = 0\) line, what happens to the metal oxide above that temperature?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
A negative \(\Delta_{\mathrm{r}}G^{\ominus}\) of formation indicates that the metal oxide is thermodynamically stable relative to the metal and \(\mathrm{O_2}\), whereas a positive \(\Delta_{\mathrm{r}}G^{\ominus}\) indicates instability.

Step 2: Evaluation
Below the temperature where the curve crosses \(\Delta_{\mathrm{r}}G^{\ominus} = 0\), the free energy of formation is negative and the oxide is stable. Above this crossing point, \(\Delta_{\mathrm{r}}G^{\ominus}\) for formation becomes positive, meaning the reverse decomposition reaction has a negative \(\Delta_{\mathrm{r}}G^{\ominus}\) and the oxide decomposes on its own.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Above the \(\Delta_{\mathrm{r}}G^{\ominus} = 0\) crossing temperature, the metal oxide decomposes on its own.

answer.text: The metal oxide becomes maximally stable and cannot be reduced.

The metal oxide sublimes without chemical decomposition.
The free energy of formation becomes positive and the oxide decomposes on its own.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_UNIT6_Q29 - Limitations of Ellingham diagram

questiontext.text: Which of the following is a limitation of the Ellingham diagram?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Ellingham diagrams are constructed solely from thermodynamic quantities (\(\Delta_{\mathrm{r}}G^{\ominus}\)) and equilibrium assumptions (\(\Delta G^{\ominus} = -RT\ln K\)).

Step 2: Evaluation
An Ellingham diagram indicates whether a reduction is thermodynamically possible, but it does not explain the kinetics (how fast the reduction proceeds). Moreover, it assumes equilibrium between reactants and products, which is not always true when species are solids or in short contact during commercial processes.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The Ellingham diagram does not explain the kinetics (rate) of the reduction process.

answer.text: It does not explain the kinetics (rate) of the reduction process.
It cannot be constructed for metal oxides, only for sulphides.
It cannot predict the minimum temperature required for reduction.
It fails to account for phase changes such as melting of the metal.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_UNIT6_Q30 - Activation energy barrier in aluminothermic reduction

questiontext.text: The reaction \(\mathrm{Cr_2O_3} + 2\mathrm{Al} \rightarrow \mathrm{Al_2O_3} + 2\mathrm{Cr}\) (\(\Delta_{\mathrm{r}}G^{\ominus} = -421\,\mathrm{kJ}\)) is thermodynamically feasible, yet it does not take place at room temperature. Why?

Thermodynamic feasibility (\(\Delta_{\mathrm{r}}G^{\ominus} < 0\)) indicates that a reaction can occur, but kinetic factors determine whether it proceeds at an observable rate at a given temperature.

Step 2: Evaluation
Even for thermodynamically feasible reactions, a certain amount of activation energy is essential to initiate the reaction, especially when the reactants are solids. Therefore, heating is required to overcome the activation energy barrier.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
A certain amount of activation energy is required for the reaction to proceed, so heating is necessary.

answer.text: Aluminium is less reactive than chromium at room temperature.
A certain amount of activation energy is essential, so heating is required.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_UNIT6_Q31 - Better reducing agent at 673 K

questiontext.text: Out of \(\mathrm{C}\) and \(\mathrm{CO}\), which is a better reducing agent for iron oxides at \(673\,\mathrm{K}\)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
In an Ellingham diagram, the reducing agent whose oxidation curve lies lower (more negative \(\Delta_{\mathrm{r}}G^{\ominus}\) per mole of \(\mathrm{O_2}\)) at a given temperature is the better reducing agent.

Step 2: Evaluation
At \(673\,\mathrm{K}\) (\(400\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}\)), the \(\Delta_{\mathrm{r}}G^{\ominus}\) line for \(2\mathrm{CO} + \mathrm{O_2} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{CO_2}\) lies below both the \(\mathrm{C, CO}\) line and the \(\mathrm{Fe, FeO}\) line (and below the iron oxide lines). Thus, \(\mathrm{CO}\) is oxidised to \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) with a larger negative \(\Delta_{\mathrm{r}}G^{\ominus}\), making \(\mathrm{CO}\) the better reducing agent at \(673\,\mathrm{K}\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
At \(673\,\mathrm{K}\), \(\mathrm{CO}\) is a better reducing agent than \(\mathrm{C}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_UNIT6_Q32 - Feasibility of Cr2O3 reduction by Al

questiontext.text: The standard Gibbs energy of formation (\(\Delta_{\mathrm{f}}G^{\ominus}\)) of \(\mathrm{Cr_2O_3}\) is \(-540\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}\) and that of \(\mathrm{Al_2O_3}\) is \(-827\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}\). What is \(\Delta_{\mathrm{r}}G^{\ominus}\) for the reduction \(\mathrm{Cr_2O_3}(\mathrm{s}) + 2\mathrm{Al}(\mathrm{s}) \rightarrow \mathrm{Al_2O_3}(\mathrm{s}) + 2\mathrm{Cr}(\mathrm{s})\), and is the reaction thermodynamically feasible?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
\(\Delta_{\mathrm{f}}G^{\ominus}(\mathrm{Cr_2O_3}) = -540\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}\)
\(\Delta_{\mathrm{f}}G^{\ominus}(\mathrm{Al_2O_3}) = -827\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}\)
Target reaction: \(\mathrm{Cr_2O_3}(\mathrm{s}) + 2\mathrm{Al}(\mathrm{s}) \rightarrow \mathrm{Al_2O_3}(\mathrm{s}) + 2\mathrm{Cr}(\mathrm{s})\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
For elements in their standard states (\(\mathrm{Al}(\mathrm{s})\) and \(\mathrm{Cr}(\mathrm{s})\)), \(\Delta_{\mathrm{f}}G^{\ominus} = 0\). A reaction is thermodynamically feasible if \(\Delta_{\mathrm{r}}G^{\ominus} < 0\).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
\(\Delta_{\mathrm{r}}G^{\ominus} = \sum \Delta_{\mathrm{f}}G^{\ominus}(\text{products}) - \sum \Delta_{\mathrm{f}}G^{\ominus}(\text{reactants})\).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
\(\Delta_{\mathrm{r}}G^{\ominus} = \Delta_{\mathrm{f}}G^{\ominus}(\mathrm{Al_2O_3}) - \Delta_{\mathrm{f}}G^{\ominus}(\mathrm{Cr_2O_3})\)
\(\Delta_{\mathrm{r}}G^{\ominus} = (-827\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}) - (-540\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}})\)
\(\Delta_{\mathrm{r}}G^{\ominus} = -827 + 540 = -287\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}\).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Since \(\Delta_{\mathrm{r}}G^{\ominus} = -287\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}\) is negative, the reduction of \(\mathrm{Cr_2O_3}\) by \(\mathrm{Al}\) is thermodynamically feasible.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_UNIT6_Q34 - Why CO cannot reduce ZnO

The \(\mathrm{CO, CO_2}\) curve lies above the \(\mathrm{Zn, ZnO}\) curve in the Ellingham diagram, whereas the \(\mathrm{C, CO}\) curve lies below it at \(1673\,\mathrm{K}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_UNIT6_Q36 - Calculating Gibbs energy for FeO reduction at 1673 K

questiontext.text: At \(1673\,\mathrm{K}\), \(\Delta_{\mathrm{r}}G^{\ominus}\) for \(2\mathrm{FeO} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{Fe} + \mathrm{O_2}\) is \(+341\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}\) and \(\Delta_{\mathrm{r}}G^{\ominus}\) for \(2\mathrm{C} + \mathrm{O_2} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{CO}\) is \(-447\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}\). What is \(\Delta_{\mathrm{r}}G^{\ominus}\) for the reaction \(\mathrm{FeO}(\mathrm{s}) + \mathrm{C}(\mathrm{s}) \rightarrow \mathrm{Fe}(\mathrm{s/l}) + \mathrm{CO}(\mathrm{g})\)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
At \(1673\,\mathrm{K}\):
\(2\mathrm{FeO} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{Fe} + \mathrm{O_2}\), \(\Delta_{\mathrm{r}}G_1^{\ominus} = +341\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}\)
\(2\mathrm{C} + \mathrm{O_2} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{CO}\), \(\Delta_{\mathrm{r}}G_2^{\ominus} = -447\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Standard Gibbs energy changes are additive when chemical equations are combined, and scaling a chemical equation by a factor scales \(\Delta_{\mathrm{r}}G^{\ominus}\) by the same factor.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Coupling the two reactions cancels \(\mathrm{O_2}(\mathrm{g})\) and gives the net \(\Delta_{\mathrm{r}}G^{\ominus} = \Delta_{\mathrm{r}}G_1^{\ominus} + \Delta_{\mathrm{r}}G_2^{\ominus}\) for \(2\,\mathrm{mol}\) of \(\mathrm{FeO}\).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Adding the two equations:
\(2\mathrm{FeO} + 2\mathrm{C} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{Fe} + 2\mathrm{CO}\)
\(\Delta_{\mathrm{r}}G^{\ominus} = (+341) + (-447) = -106\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}\).
Dividing by \(2\) for \(1\,\mathrm{mol}\) of \(\mathrm{FeO}\):
\(\mathrm{FeO} + \mathrm{C} \rightarrow \mathrm{Fe} + \mathrm{CO}\)
\(\Delta_{\mathrm{r}}G^{\ominus} = \frac{-106}{2} = -53\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}\).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The negative value \(-53\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}\) confirms that reduction of \(\mathrm{FeO}\) by coke is feasible at \(1673\,\mathrm{K}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_UNIT6_Q37 - Conditions for Al reducing MgO and Mg reducing Al2O3

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_UNIT6_Q38 - Effect of liquid metal product on reduction

questiontext.text: Why is the reduction of a solid metal oxide thermodynamically easier if the metal formed is in the liquid state at the temperature of reduction?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The feasibility of reduction is governed by \(\Delta_{\mathrm{r}}G^{\ominus} = \Delta_{\mathrm{r}}H^{\ominus} - T\Delta_{\mathrm{r}}S^{\ominus}\).

Entropy is higher when the metal product is in the liquid state than in the solid state. Step 3: Final Conclusion
The higher entropy of the liquid metal makes \(\Delta S\) more positive and \(\Delta_{\mathrm{r}}G^{\ominus}\) more negative, making reduction easier.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_UNIT6_Q46 - Extraction of chlorine from brine

questiontext.text: For the extraction of chlorine from brine, \(2\mathrm{Cl^-}(\mathrm{aq}) + 2\mathrm{H_2O}(\mathrm{l}) \rightarrow 2\mathrm{OH^-}(\mathrm{aq}) + \mathrm{H_2}(\mathrm{g}) + \mathrm{Cl_2}(\mathrm{g})\), \(\Delta G^{\ominus} = +422\,\mathrm{kJ}\). Using \(\Delta G^{\ominus} = -nE^{\ominus}F\) (with \(n = 2\) and \(F = 96500\,\mathrm{C\,mol^{-1}}\)), what is \(E^{\ominus}\) and what minimum external emf is required?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
\(\Delta G^{\ominus} = +422\,\mathrm{kJ} = +422000\,\mathrm{J}\)
\(n = 2\) electrons transferred
\(F \approx 96500\,\mathrm{C\,mol^{-1}}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
A positive \(\Delta G^{\ominus}\) corresponds to a negative \(E^{\ominus}\), meaning the reaction is non-spontaneous and requires an external emf greater than \(|E^{\ominus}|\) (plus any excess potential to overcome hindering reactions).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
\(\Delta G^{\ominus} = -nE^{\ominus}F \implies E^{\ominus} = -\frac{\Delta G^{\ominus}}{nF}\).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
\(E^{\ominus} = -\frac{422000\,\mathrm{J}}{2 \times 96500\,\mathrm{C\,mol^{-1}}} = -\frac{422000}{193000} \approx -2.19\,\mathrm{V} \approx -2.2\,\mathrm{V}\).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Since \(E^{\ominus} = -2.2\,\mathrm{V}\), the electrolysis requires an external emf greater than \(2.2\,\mathrm{V}\) (along with excess potential to overcome hindering reactions).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_UNIT6_Q47 - Electrolysis of aqueous NaCl versus molten NaCl

questiontext.text: How do the products of electrolysis of aqueous \(\mathrm{NaCl}\) (brine) differ from those of molten \(\mathrm{NaCl}\)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
In aqueous electrolysis, water participates in the cathode reaction instead of \(\mathrm{Na^+}\) because \(\mathrm{Na^+}\) has a much more negative reduction potential than water.

Step 2: Evaluation
Electrolysis of aqueous \(\mathrm{NaCl}\) (brine) produces \(\mathrm{Cl_2}\) gas along with \(\mathrm{H_2}\) gas and aqueous \(\mathrm{NaOH}\) as by-products. In contrast, electrolysis of molten \(\mathrm{NaCl}\) (in the absence of water) produces metallic \(\mathrm{Na}\) instead of \(\mathrm{NaOH}\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Aqueous \(\mathrm{NaCl}\) electrolysis gives \(\mathrm{Cl_2}\), \(\mathrm{H_2}\), and \(\mathrm{NaOH}(\mathrm{aq})\), whereas molten \(\mathrm{NaCl}\) electrolysis produces \(\mathrm{Na}\) metal (and \(\mathrm{Cl_2}\)) instead of \(\mathrm{NaOH}\).

answer.text: Aqueous \(\mathrm{NaCl}\) gives \(\mathrm{Cl_2}\) with \(\mathrm{H_2}\) and \(\mathrm{NaOH}(\mathrm{aq})\) as by-products, whereas molten \(\mathrm{NaCl}\) produces \(\mathrm{Na}\) metal and not \(\mathrm{NaOH}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_UNIT6_Q48 - Elements in anode mud during copper refining

questiontext.text: In the electrolytic refining of blister copper using acidified \(\mathrm{CuSO_4}\) solution, which elements are deposited as anode mud?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
During electrolytic refining, more basic (more reactive) metal impurities dissolve into the electrolytic bath, while less basic (less reactive) impurities do not oxidise and fall to the bottom as anode mud.

Step 2: Evaluation
Impurities from blister copper that deposit as anode mud include antimony, selenium, tellurium, silver, gold, and platinum. Recovery of these valuable elements often meets the cost of refining.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Anode mud contains antimony, selenium, tellurium, silver, gold, and platinum.

answer.text: Antimony, selenium, tellurium, silver, gold, and platinum

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_UNIT6_Q49 - Mond process for refining nickel

questiontext.text: In the Mond process for refining nickel, impure nickel is heated in a stream of \(\mathrm{CO}\) at \(330\text{--}350\,\mathrm{K}\) to form a volatile complex, which is then decomposed at \(450\text{--}470\,\mathrm{K}\) to give pure nickel. What is this volatile complex?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The Mond process is a vapour phase refining technique in which nickel forms a volatile carbonyl complex with carbon monoxide.

Step 2: Evaluation
Nickel reacts with carbon monoxide at \(330\text{--}350\,\mathrm{K}\) to form volatile nickel tetracarbonyl: \(\mathrm{Ni} + 4\mathrm{CO} \xrightarrow{330\text{--}350\,\mathrm{K}} \mathrm{Ni(CO)_4}\). This complex decomposes at \(450\text{--}470\,\mathrm{K}\) to yield pure nickel and regenerate \(\mathrm{CO}\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The volatile complex formed in the Mond process is \(\mathrm{Ni(CO)_4}\) (nickel tetracarbonyl).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_UNIT6_Q50 - van Arkel method for refining Zr and Ti

questiontext.text: The van Arkel method is very useful for removing oxygen and nitrogen impurities from metals such as \(\mathrm{Zr}\) and \(\mathrm{Ti}\). Which reagent and filament temperature are used in this process?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
In the van Arkel method, the crude metal is converted into a volatile covalent iodide in an evacuated vessel and then thermally decomposed on a heated filament.

Step 2: Evaluation
Crude zirconium or titanium is heated with iodine (\(\mathrm{I_2}\)) to form volatile \(\mathrm{ZrI_4}\) (or \(\mathrm{TiI_4}\)). The metal iodide is then decomposed on a tungsten filament electrically heated to about \(1800\,\mathrm{K}\), depositing pure metal on the filament.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The van Arkel method uses iodine (\(\mathrm{I_2}\)) and a tungsten filament heated to about \(1800\,\mathrm{K}\).

Iodine and a tungsten filament at about \(1800\,\mathrm{K}\)

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_UNIT6_Q51 - Suitability of column chromatography in refining

questiontext.text: Which refining method is most suitable when an element is available in minute quantities and the impurities present have chemical properties very close to those of the element to be purified?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
When chemical properties of an element and its impurities are nearly identical and only minute quantities are available, conventional chemical separation or melting/boiling methods are ineffective.

Step 2: Evaluation
Column chromatography is specifically suited for purifying elements available in minute quantities when the impurities do not differ greatly in chemical properties from the element to be purified.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Column chromatography is the most suitable refining method in this case.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_UNIT6_Q52 - Two requirements for vapour phase refining

questiontext.text: What are the two essential requirements for a metal to be purified by vapour phase refining?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Vapour phase refining purifies a metal by converting it into a gaseous compound that is transported away from non-volatile impurities and then decomposed back into pure metal.

Step 2: Evaluation
The two essential requirements are: (i) the metal should form a volatile compound with an available reagent, and (ii) the volatile compound should be easily decomposable so that recovery of the pure metal is easy.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The metal must form a volatile compound with an available reagent, and that volatile compound must be easily decomposable.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_UNIT6_Q53 - Uses of aluminium, zinc, and alloy steels

questiontext.text: Which statement regarding the industrial uses of aluminium, zinc, and iron alloys is INCORRECT?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Metals and their alloys are selected for specific industrial uses based on reactivity, corrosion resistance, hardness, and mechanical properties.

Step 2: Evaluation
Aluminium, being highly reactive, is used in the extraction of chromium and manganese from their oxides. Zinc is used for galvanising iron and in batteries. Nickel steel is used for making cables, automobiles, aeroplane parts, pendulums, and measuring tapes. However, chrome steel—not wrought iron—is used for cutting tools and crushing machines, while wrought iron is used for anchors, wires, bolts, chains, and agricultural implements.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The statement that wrought iron is used for cutting tools and crushing machines is incorrect.

answer.text: Wrought iron is used for cutting tools and crushing machines, whereas chrome steel is used for anchors and chains.
Aluminium is used in the extraction of chromium and manganese from their oxides.
Zinc is used for galvanising iron and in large quantities in batteries.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_UNIT6_Q54 - Composition of German silver alloy

questiontext.text: What is the percentage composition of German silver?

German silver is a zinc-containing copper-nickel alloy despite its name.

German silver contains \(\mathrm{Cu}\) (\(25\text{--}30\%\)), \(\mathrm{Zn}\) (\(25\text{--}30\%\)), and \(\mathrm{Ni}\) (\(40\text{--}50\%\)), and contains no silver (\(\mathrm{Ag}\)).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
German silver consists of \(\mathrm{Cu}\) (\(25\text{--}30\%\)), \(\mathrm{Zn}\) (\(25\text{--}30\%\)), and \(\mathrm{Ni}\) (\(40\text{--}50\%\)).
